s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: (title for God; a Greek transliteration of an Aramaic word meaning ‘father’) one who combines aspects of supernatural authority and care for his people
s.c: Though there is a widespread tendency to preserve the Aramaic transliteration in the form of either abba or aba, there are frequent dangers in doing so, since the transliterated form may actually correspond to another word in a receptor language and thus provide an obstacle to proper understanding. In general, there is no point in a translation of ἀββά, since the resulting expression would simply be Father Father. Accordingly, in many languages the combination of Abba, Father is simply reduced to Father. In a number of languages, however, a vocative form (that is to say, a form used in direct address) is different from a form used in speaking about God as Father. It is, of course, essential to employ the appropriate grammatical form.|In a number of languages it is necessary to distinguish clearly between ‘Father’ when referring to the heavenly Father and ‘father’ as a reference to a human father. The use of capitalization is quite satisfactory for the individual who is reading a text but not for one who is hearing it read, and since more people hear a text read than read it for themselves, it is essential that the reference of ‘Father’ be clear. In order to identify the use of ‘Father’ as a title for God, it is possible in many languages to use ‘Father in heaven’ or ‘Father above’ or ‘Father God.’|In some languages it may even be necessary to identify the ‘Father’ as the creator and therefore employ a phrase such as ‘our Father who created us.’|A particularly complicating factor involved in the use of ‘Father’ as a title for God is its occurrence without a pronominal reference as to whose father is involved. For example, in a number of languages one cannot speak of ‘father’ without indicating whose father, because a person does not become a father except by some relationship to another individual. Therefore, one must always speak of ‘my father’ or ‘his father’ and never simply ‘the father.’ In passages in which Jesus is speaking of ‘the Father’ in relationship to himself, it is necessary usually to employ a phrase such as ‘my Father.’ When, however, ‘Father’ is used as a title for ‘God’ in his relationship to people generally, then one may speak of ‘our Father’ (normally with an inclusive first person plural pronoun if the language in question makes a distinction between inclusive and exclusive first person plural pronoun referents).

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Regions Above the Earth
s.d: (an idiom, literally: Abraham’s bosom) the heavenly abode, with the implication of close interpersonal relations
s.c: A literal rendering of κόλπος Ἀβραάμ as ‘the bosom of Abraham’ or ‘the lap of Abraham’ is often misleading. In some languages it may even suggest homosexuality, and in other cases it implies that Lazarus was either a baby or was changed into a baby in heaven. Since κόλπος Ἀβραάμ is generally interpreted as a reference to the eschatological heavenly feast, one may be justified in rendering ⟦Luke 16:22|Luke 16:22⟧ as in TEV “the poor man died and was carried by the angels to sit beside Abraham at the feast in heaven.” In some languages κόλπος Ἀβραάμ in this context is translated as ‘he was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side’ or ‘… to be with Abraham.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Love, Affection, Compassion
s.d: to have love for someone or something, based on sincere appreciation and high regard
s.g: to love; to regard with affection; loving concern; love
s.c: Though some persons have tried to assign certain significant differences of meaning between ἀγαπάω, ἀγάπη and φιλέω, φιλία (LN 25.33), it does not seem possible to insist upon a contrast of meaning in any and all contexts. For example, the usage in ⟦John 21:15|John 21:15⟧, ⟦John 21:16|John 21:16⟧, ⟦John 21:17|John 21:17⟧, ⟦John 21:17|John 21:17⟧, ⟦John 21:17|John 21:17⟧ seems to reflect simply a rhetorical alternation designed to avoid undue repetition. There is, however, one significant clue to possible meaningful differences in at least some contexts, namely, the fact that people are never commanded to love one another with φιλέω or φιλία, but only with ἀγαπάω and ἀγάπη. Though the meanings of these terms overlap considerably in many contexts, there are probably some significant differences in certain contexts; that is to say, φιλέω and φιλία are likely to focus upon love or affection based upon interpersonal association, while ἀγαπάω and ἀγάπη focus upon love and affection based on deep appreciation and high regard. On the basis of this type of distinction, one can understand some of the reasons for the use of ἀγαπάω and ἀγάπη in commands to Christians to love one another. It would, however, be quite wrong to assume that φιλέω and φιλία refer only to human love, while ἀγαπάω and ἀγάπη refer to divine love. Both sets of terms are used for the total range of loving relations between people, between people and God, and between God and Jesus Christ.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink

s.c: The meaning of ἀγάπη may be rendered in some languages as meals in which you show your love for one another as you eat together or your eating together as the result of your love for one another.

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Love, Affection, Compassion
s.d: (derivative of {L:ἀγαπάω<SDBG:ἀγαπάω:000000>}[a] ‘to love,’ {D:25.43}) pertaining to one who or that which is loved
s.g: object of one’s affection; one who is loved; beloved; dear
s.c: It is also possible to understand ἀγαπητός in ⟦Matthew 12:18|Matthew 12:18⟧ as ‘the only beloved one’ (see LN 58.53), and the meaning may, in fact, be simply ‘only’ or ‘unique.’ This meaning has evidently arisen because of the association of ἀγαπητός with μονογενής ‘unique, only’ (LN 58.52).

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: a supernatural being that attends upon or serves as a messenger of a superior supernatural entity
s.c: In many languages a term for ‘angels’ is borrowed from another dominant language, but in other instances a somewhat descriptive phrase may be employed. The most common expressions for the ‘angels of God’ are ‘messengers’ and ‘messengers from heaven.’ Sometimes these angels are called ‘spirit messengers’ and even ‘flying messengers.’ In some instances they have been called ‘the holy servants of God,’ but an expression such as ‘servants of God’ or even ‘messengers of God’ tends to overlap in meaning with expressions used to characterize the role and function of the prophets who were sent as messengers from God. In some languages a term for ‘angels’ is contrasted with that for ‘prophets’ by calling angels ‘messengers from heaven’ and prophets ‘messengers from God.’ The ‘angels of the Devil’ are often called ‘the Devil’s servants.’|One cannot avoid problems involved in the rendering of ‘angel’ merely by borrowing a term. In some instances such a borrowing may already exist in the language and with a different meaning. For example, in one instance 'angel' had already been borrowed but with a meaning of babies who died at childbirth or shortly thereafter.

s.dp: Animals
s.d: collective for a group of animals
s.c: In a number of languages a ‘herd’ must be translated merely as ‘many,’ since there is frequently no corresponding collective term which would be applicable only or even primarily to pigs. In some languages, however, there are highly specific terms for various types of groups of animals, so that a distinctive collective expression may be used for pigs, sheep, horses, camels, etc.

s.c: Though in certain contexts ἁγιάζω and ἁγιασμός suggest resulting moral behavior, the emphasis is not upon a manner of life but upon religious activity and observances which reflect one’s dedication or consecration to God. Accordingly, in ⟦1 Corinthians 1:2|1 Corinthians 1:2⟧ one may translate ἁγιάζω as who have given themselves to God or who serve God with a whole heart.

s.g: to hallow; to regard as holy; to honor as holy
s.c: In a number of languages it is impossible to employ an expression such as ‘your name’ as a reference for God himself. Therefore, it may be necessary to translate this expression in ⟦Matthew 6:9|Matthew 6:9⟧ as ‘may you be reverenced as holy’ or even ‘may you be acknowledged as God.’

s.dp: Religious Activities › Dedicate, Consecrate

Accordingly, in ⟦1 Corinthians 1:2|1 Corinthians 1:2⟧ one may translate ἁγιάζω as ‘who have given themselves to God’ or ‘who serve God with a whole heart.’

s.dp: Religious Activities › Dedicate, Consecrate
s.d: pertaining to being dedicated or consecrated to the service of God
s.c: In some languages it is essential to distinguish between ἅγιος and ὅσιος when these refer to God (see LN 88.24) and when they refer to persons or objects which have been consecrated to the service of God. It is both theoretically and practically advantageous to make a significant distinction in meaning on the basis of these contextual differences which occur in the Greek NT. It is not difficult to translate ἅγιος and ὅσιος by expressions meaning ‘dedicated to God,’ ‘devout,’ ‘pious,’ etc., but it may be extremely difficult to translate ἅγιος and ὅσιος when applied to God. In some languages one can only use an expression such as ‘he who is truly God’ or ‘he who is in every respect God.’

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Religious
s.d: persons who belong to God, and as such constitute a religious entity
s.c: In rendering οἱ ἅγιοι it is important to avoid an expression which means ‘sanctified,’ for the focus is not upon a particular state of holiness, but upon a special relationship with God. Those who are spoken of as οἱ ἅγιοι may also be admonished to become sanctified.|In a number of respects, οἱ ἅγιοι is similar in meaning to λαός 'people of God' (LN 11.12) and to ἀδελφός 'fellow believer' (LN 11.23).

s.c: ἅγιος and ἅγιος should be translated in essentially the same way as ναός (LN 7.15).

s.dp: Constructions › Parts and Areas of Buildings
s.d: the interior (either the outer or the inner of the two rooms) of the sanctuary of the Jerusalem Temple or of the earlier tabernacle or of a corresponding ‘spiritual holy place,’ perhaps regarded as being in heaven
s.c: The inner room was more specifically identified by the phrase ἅγια ἁγίων, literally ‘holy of holies’ ⟦Hebrews 9:3|Hebrews 9:3⟧, a Hebrew idiom indicating superlative degree. The inner sanctuary could also be referred to as ‘within the curtain’ (τὸ ἐσώτερον τοῦ καταπετάσματος ⟦Hebrews 6:19|Hebrews 6:19⟧). See ἅγιος (LN 88.24) and LN 7.18.|The outer room of the sanctuary may be referred to in some languages as simply ‘the first room of the Holy Temple’ or ‘the first holy room of the Temple.’ The holy of holies may be referred to as ‘the most holy place’ or ‘the second holy room of the Temple’ or ‘the interior holy room of the Temple.’ What is important here is the degree of holiness, not so much the actual location within the Temple. It is for this reason that for the ‘holy of holies’ many translators use ‘the most sacred place’ or ‘the very, very sacred room.’ In this type of context the term ‘sacred’ may be rendered as ‘dedicated especially to God’ or ‘consecrated to God.’

s.dp: Artifacts › Instruments Used in Fishing
s.d: small, curved piece of metal or bone or even a strong thorn, with a sharp point on one end, usually with a barb just behind the point, and a loop or bend on the other end to which a fishing line can be attached; used with some bait attached to it in order to attract a fish
s.c: A literal rendering of ⟦Matthew 17:27|Matthew 17:27⟧ could be quite misleading, since it would imply that only the hook was thrown into the water. What was thrown into the water was a line with a baited hook on the end, and it may be necessary to be explicit in some languages in order to avoid misunderstanding.

s.c: ἀγορά differs in meaning from ἐμπόριον (LN 57.206) in that the focus is upon a commercial center involving a number of places for doing business. The term ἐμπόριον may be used to refer to the same type of geographical location, but the focus is upon the activity and not the place.

s.dp: Control, Rule › Release, Set Free
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:ἀγοράζω<SDBG:ἀγοράζω:000000>}[a] ‘to buy,’ {D:57.188}) to cause the release or freedom of someone by a means which proves costly to the individual causing the release
s.c: A literal rendering of ἀγοράζω or ἐξαγοράζω as ‘to release by means of paying a price’ can be misinterpreted in the sense that Christ actually engaged in some kind of monetary transaction. A literal translation may also lead to the mistaken interpretation, which was widespread in the Middle Ages, that in redeeming the believers God actually paid a price to the Devil. Obviously, ἀγοράζω in ⟦1 Corinthians 6:20|1 Corinthians 6:20⟧ and ἐξαγοράζω in ⟦Galatians 3:13|Galatians 3:13⟧ must be understood in a figurative sense.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Laziness, Idleness
s.d: (derivative of {L:ἀγορά<SDBG:ἀγορά:000000>} ‘marketplace,’ {D:57.207}) a person who habitually idles in the marketplace

s.dp: Courts and Legal Procedures › Court of Justice
s.d: a court of justice for determining guilt or innocence{N:001}
s.c: For languages which do not have technical terms for a court, it is usually possible to use some such phrase as ‘to be brought before a judge’ or ‘to have judges decide one’s case.’

s.dp: Attachment › Grasp, Hold
s.d: the act of catching something
s.c: Though in Greek the term ἄγρα may be used to refer to the catching of a wide variety of objects, in the context of ⟦Luke 5:4|Luke 5:4⟧ the reference is to fish, and one must make certain that the appropriate term in the receptor language is employed, depending, for example, whether one catches fish, animals, or people.

s.dp: Learn
s.d: pertaining to one who has not acquired a formal education (referring primarily to formal training)
s.c: Some persons have assumed that ἀγράμματος in ⟦Acts 4:13|Acts 4:13⟧ means ‘illiterate’ in the sense of not being able to read or write, but this is highly unlikely in view of the almost universal literacy in NT times, and especially as the result of extensive synagogue schools. Evidently, ἀγράμματος in ⟦Acts 4:13|Acts 4:13⟧ refers to a lack of formal rabbinic training.

s.dp: Existence in Space › Remain, Stay
s.d: to spend time outdoors, with the possible implication of living outdoors

s.dp: Learn › Learn Something Against Someone
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of term meaning literally: ‘to hunt, to trap,’ not occurring in the NT) to acquire information about an error or fault, with the purpose of causing harm or trouble
s.g: to trap; to catch off guard; to catch in a mistake
s.c: In a number of languages it is possible to retain the figurative meaning of ‘trap’ or ‘catch,’ but in a number of instances other figures are used, for example, ‘to cause to trip,’ ‘to cause to fall,’ ‘to hear wrong words from his mouth,’ or ‘to use his words against him.’

s.dp: Plants › Trees
s.d: a tree regarded by some (though probably wrongly) as the ancestor of the domestic olive tree; smaller, produces smaller fruit with less oil than domestic variety; Olea europaea sylvestris
s.c: In speaking of the wild olive tree as ‘an uncultivated olive tree,’ it is important to make clear that it is not the matter of neglect which produces the wild tree, but the fact that such a tree is essentially different from the cultivated one. A marginal note to this effect may be useful in the context of ⟦Romans 11:17|Romans 11:17⟧. The precise identification of the ‘wild olive tree’ cannot be made with certainty. It may be possible in some instances to speak of such a tree as an ‘uncultivated olive tree’ in contrast with a ‘cultivated olive tree.’ It may also be possible to speak of the wild olive tree as ‘the olive tree producing bitter fruit,’ although in reality all olives are bitter before they are cured.|This reference in ⟦Romans 11:17|Romans 11:17⟧ is intentionally strange because the usual course of action was to graft cultivated branches into wild trees.

s.dp: Violence, Harm, Destroy, Kill › Violence
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἄγριος ‘wild, savage’) pertaining to what is violent and uncontrolled
s.c: This expression in ⟦Jude 1:13|Jude 1:13⟧, however, is applied to people, and therefore it may be necessary to make the figurative reference clear, for example, they are like stormy waves of the sea or … wild waves of the sea.

s.d: pertaining to what is undomesticated and uncultivated in nature

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: Herod Agrippa II, the son of Herod Agrippa I (see {S:04401200100000})

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Pastures and Cultivated Lands
s.d: land under cultivation or used for pasture

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Areas Which Are Uninhabited or Only Sparsely Populated
s.d: a rural area in contrast with a population center
s.c: A rural area is often identified by a term or phrase meaning ‘extension of fields’ or ‘place of field after field’ or ‘area of farms.’

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Population Centers
s.d: a relatively small village, possibly merely a cluster of farms

s.dp: Learn › Be Ready To Learn, Pay Attention
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἀγρυπνέω ‘to keep oneself awake,’ not occurring in the NT) to make an effort to learn of what might be a potential future threat
s.g: to be alert; to be on the lookout for; to be vigilant

s.dp: Help, Care For › Care For, Take Care Of
s.d: to take care of or to look after, with the implication of continuous and wakeful concern for
s.g: to look after; to take care of

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sleep, Waking
s.d: the state of remaining awake because of not being able to go to sleep, whether from anxiety or because of external circumstances
s.c: In the two occurrences of ἀγρυπνία in the NT (⟦2 Corinthians 6:5|2 Corinthians 6:5⟧, ⟦2 Corinthians 11:27|2 Corinthians 11:27⟧), failure to sleep was evidently the result of external circumstances which prevented normal sleep. It may therefore be possible to translate ἀγρυπνία as it was not possible to sleep or there was no way to sleep.

s.dp: Linear Movement › Lead, Bring, Take
s.d: to direct or guide the movement of an object, without special regard to point of departure or goal
s.c: The Spirit of God is also regarded as an agent in leading or directing the movement of a person, for example, ἤγετο ἐν τῷ πνεύματι ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ he was led by the Spirit into the desert (⟦Luke 4:1|Luke 4:1⟧).|ἄγω also occurs in contexts in which the leading involves force: ὅταν ἄγωσιν ὑμᾶς παραδιδόντες whenever you are taken into custody and turned over to the courts (⟦Mark 13:11|Mark 13:11⟧); Ἤγοντο δὲ καὶ ἕτεροι κακοῦργοι δύο σὺν αὐτῷ ἀναιρεθῆναι they led two others off also, both of them criminals, to be put to death with him (⟦Luke 23:32|Luke 23:32⟧).

s.dp: Linear Movement › Carry, Bear
s.d: to carry or bring, especially animate beings{N:001}

s.dp: Linear Movement › Leave, Depart, Flee, Escape, Send
s.d: to move away from a reference point
s.c: It would also be possible to translate ἄγωμεν in ⟦John 11:7|John 11:7⟧ as let us depart for.

s.dp: Guide, Discipline, Follow › Guide, Lead
s.d: to so influence others as to cause them to follow a recommended course of action
s.g: to guide; to direct; to lead
s.c: In some languages it is difficult to distinguish readily between expressions for ‘leading’ and those which refer to ‘ruling’ or ‘governing,’ but it is important to try to distinguish clearly between these two different sets of interpersonal relations. In some languages, the concept of ‘leading’ can be expressed by ‘showing how to’ or ‘demonstrating how one ought to.’ In other languages it is possible to speak of ‘leading’ as simply ‘going ahead of,’ but too often such an expression may designate only ‘a scout’ who goes ahead to see whether things are safe, or it may refer only to a person who insists on his prerogative as the most distinguished person in a group.

s.dp: Perform, Do › Function
s.d: to be actively performing some function
s.g: to carry on; to function; to be operative
s.c: In some languages the equivalent of ‘the courts are functioning’ is ‘the courts are open’ or ‘the judges are on duty’ or ‘the officials are listening to complaints.’

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: to occur at a particular or expected time
s.g: to take place; to be; to occur
s.c: For another interpretation of ἄγω in ⟦Luke 24:21|Luke 24:21⟧, see LN 67.79.

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: to experience a duration of time
s.c: For another interpretation of ἄγω in ⟦Luke 24:21|Luke 24:21⟧, see LN 67.64.

s.dp: Discourse Markers › Prompters of Attention
s.d: prompter of attention, which serves also to emphasize the following statement
s.g: look; listen; pay attention; come now; then

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Behavior, Conduct
s.d: to conduct oneself, with apparent focus upon overt daily behavior{N:001}
s.g: to live; to conduct oneself; to behave; behavior; conduct

s.dp: Hostility, Strife › Strife, Struggle
s.d: to engage in intense struggle, involving physical or nonphysical force against strong opposition
s.c: In a number of languages a marked distinction is made between physical fighting and nonphysical contending with someone. It is therefore often impossible to carry over any terminology involving war or physical struggling to contexts in which one is speaking of interpersonal hostility or contention.

s.dp: Contests and Play
s.d: a race involving competition and struggle

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Sorrow, Regret
s.d: a state of great mental and emotional grief and anxiety

s.dp: Hostility, Strife › Strife, Struggle
s.d: to engage in intense struggle, involving physical or nonphysical force against strong opposition
s.c: In a number of languages a marked distinction is made between physical fighting and nonphysical contending with someone. It is therefore often impossible to carry over any terminology involving war or physical struggling to contexts in which one is speaking of interpersonal hostility or contention.

s.dp: Contests and Play
s.d: to compete in an athletic contest, with emphasis on effort

s.dp: Aspect › Do Intensely or Extensively
s.d: to strive to do something with great intensity and effort
s.g: to make every effort to; to do everything possible to; to strain oneself to

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: ancestor of the human race

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Pay, Price, Cost
s.d: pertaining to there being no charge or expenditure

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person in the genealogy of Jesus

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations of the Same Generation
s.d: a female having the same father and mother as the reference person
s.c: For a discussion of ἀδελφή in the possible meaning of cousin, see the discussion under ἀδελφός (LN 10.49).|A number of languages make a distinction in relative age of sisters, paralleling the usage of distinct terms for ‘brother’ (see LN 10.49). The order of names in the NT normally suggests relative age, and therefore in speaking of Martha and Mary in such languages, one may designate Mary as the younger sister, since the order is normally first Martha and then Mary, though in ⟦John 11:1|John 11:1⟧ the order is reversed.

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Religious
s.d: a close female associate of a group with well-defined membership (in the NT referring specifically to fellow believers in Christ)
s.g: fellow believer; sister in Christ; sister in the faith
s.c: Though in a number of languages it is possible to use a term meaning ‘sister’ in the sense of a fellow believer, in some languages this cannot be done. As in the case of ἀδελφός (see LN 11.23), it may be possible to use a term such as ‘relative,’ but more often than not, it may be necessary to use a phrase such as ‘one who also believes’ or ‘one who believes in Christ even as we do.’

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations of the Same Generation
s.d: a male having the same father (and, usually, mother) as the reference person
s.c: In a number of languages it is necessary to indicate the difference between older and younger brothers, and this can usually be done on the basis of Semitic usage, since the older brother was normally named first. Therefore, in ⟦Matthew 4:18|Matthew 4:18⟧ one may translate ‘Simon and his younger brother Andrew.’|The interpretation of ἀδελφός in such passages as ⟦Matthew 12:46|Matthew 12:46⟧, ⟦Mark 3:31|Mark 3:31⟧, ⟦John 2:12|John 2:12⟧ as meaning cousins (on the basis of a corresponding Hebrew term, which is used in certain cases to designate masculine relatives of various degrees) is not attested in Greek nor affirmed in the Greek-English lexicon edited by Arndt, Gingrich, and Danker. Such an interpretation depends primarily on ecclesiastical tradition.|Though the plural of ἀδελφός (namely, ἀδελφοί) can mean both brothers and sisters, there is no reason to believe that in ⟦Matthew 12:46|Matthew 12:46⟧, ⟦Mark 3:31|Mark 3:31⟧, ⟦John 2:12|John 2:12⟧, ⟦John 7:3|John 7:3⟧, ⟦John 7:5|John 7:5⟧, ⟦Acts 1:14|Acts 1:14⟧ the reference is to both brothers and sisters.|In ⟦Luke 8:21|Luke 8:21⟧ (μήτηρ μου καὶ ἀδελφοί μου οὗτοί εἰσιν οἱ τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ ἀκούοντες καὶ ποιοῦντες my mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and act accordingly) ἀδελφοί is used figuratively as a qualification of Jesus followers. In some languages, however, it is necessary to make more evident the qualifying relationship, for example, those who hear the word and act accordingly are my mother and my brothers or … are just like a mother and brothers to me.

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Religious
s.d: a close associate of a group of persons having a well-defined membership (in the NT ἀδελφός[b] refers specifically to fellow believers in Christ)
s.c: The masculine form ἀδελφός may include both men and women, but see also LN 11.24.|Though in a number of languages it is possible to use a corresponding term meaning ‘brother’ or ‘brothers’ in the sense of fellow believers, in some languages this cannot be done, and one must employ other types of expressions. In some instances it is possible to generalize a term meaning ‘relative’ and therefore to address or to speak of fellow Christians as ‘relatives’ rather than specifically ‘brothers and sisters.’ In most instances, however, one may only employ a phrase such as ‘those who also believe’ or ‘those who believe in Christ even as we do.’

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Religious
s.d: a person belonging to the same socio-religious entity and being of the same age group as the so-called reference person
s.g: brother; fellow countryman; fellow Jew; associate

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Political
s.d: a person who is a member of the same {L:πατριά<SDBG:πατριά:000001>}[b] or {L:φυλή<SDBG:φυλή:000001>}[b] ‘nation’ ({D:11.56})
s.c: The term ἄνδρες is often added to ἀδελφοί, constituting a lexical unit having essentially the same meaning as ἀδελφοί, but with the connotation of greater formality: ἄνδρες ἀδελφοί, ἐξὸν εἰπεῖν μετὰ παρρησίας πρὸς ὑμᾶς ‘fellow countrymen, I can speak to you quite plainly’ ⟦Acts 2:29|Acts 2:29⟧.|συμφυλέτης, and ἀδελφός may often be translated by a phrase, for example, ‘a person of the same country’ or ‘a man who belongs to the same nation’ or ‘one who is part of the same tribe.’

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Political
s.d: a person who lives close beside others and who thus by implication is a part of a so-called in-group, that is, the group with which an individual identifies both ethnically and culturally
s.c: Though in ⟦Matthew 5:22|Matthew 5:22⟧ and ⟦Luke 6:41|Luke 6:41⟧ one may translate ἀδελφός as ‘brother,’ the evident meaning is not a reference to a sibling, but to a close associate or neighbor, so that the denotation of ἀδελφός is very similar to that of γείτων, περίοικος, and πλησίον.|It may be that of the three terms γείτων, περίοικος, and πλησίον, the last is somewhat broader in meaning. At least πλησίον is used in ⟦Luke 10:27|Luke 10:27⟧ in a somewhat extended sense of ‘fellow man,’ while ἀδελφός probably suggests a more intimate or close relationship.

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Religious
s.d: an association of persons having a strong sense of unity
s.c: It is often quite impossible to speak of fellow Christians as ‘the brothers and sisters,’ since a number of receptor languages do not permit this type of extension of meaning from an underlying base meaning ‘brother’ or ‘sister.’ Therefore, it may be necessary to speak of ‘fellow believers’ or ‘those who believe together with others’ or ‘those who likewise believe.’ See also discussion at LN 11.23.

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › General Sensory Perception
s.d: pertaining to not being perceived
s.g: not evident; not perceived; unseen; unmarked
s.c: Though in Greek ἄδηλος may designate anything which is unperceived by any of the senses, in ⟦Luke 11:44|Luke 11:44⟧ the most evident sense involved would be sight, and therefore one may translate ‘because you are like graves that cannot be seen.’

s.dp: Mode › Certain, Uncertain
s.d: the uncertainty of some event or state

s.dp: Think › To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
s.d: pertaining to being without a special goal or purpose
s.c: In a number of languages ‘aimlessly’ may be rendered simply as ‘without having some goal’ or ‘without some reason’ or ‘without trying to accomplish something.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Worry, Anxiety, Distress, Peace
s.d: to be distressed and troubled, with the probable implication of anguish
s.g: to be troubled; to be upset; to be distressed

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Regions Below the Surface of the Earth
s.d: a place or abode of the dead, including both the righteous and the unrighteous (in most contexts ᾅδης[a] is equivalent to the Hebrew term Sheol)
s.g: the world of the dead; Hades
s.c: There are several problems involved in rendering ᾅδης as world of the dead, since in some languages this may be interpreted as suggesting that there are two different earths, one for the living and another for the dead. In such cases, ᾅδης may be more satisfactorily rendered as ‘where the dead are’ or ‘where the dead remain.’|In ⟦Luke 16:23|Luke 16:23⟧ ᾅδης obviously involves torment and punishment. These aspects are important supplementary features of the word ᾅδης but are not integral elements of the meaning. In ⟦Luke 16:23|Luke 16:23⟧, however, it may be appropriate to use a term which is equivalent to Greek γέεννα meaning hell (see LN 1.21). It is indeed possible that in addressing a GrecoRoman audience Luke would have used ᾅδης in a context implying punishment and torment, since this was a typical Greco-Roman view of the next world. But since Luke also uses γέεννα, as in ⟦Luke 12:5|Luke 12:5⟧, it is possible that the choice of ᾅδης in ⟦Luke 16:23|Luke 16:23⟧ reflects Luke’s intent to emphasize the fact that ᾅδης includes both the unrighteous and the righteous.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ᾅδης<SDBG:ᾅδης:000000>}[a] Hades, {D:1.19}, as a personification of the power of Hades as the place of the dead)
s.c: In ⟦1 Corinthians 15:55|1 Corinthians 15:55⟧ ᾅδη is a variant reading in the apparatus of θάνατε ‘death’ (LN 23.99).|In some languages it is extremely difficult to personify death except as a reference to some demon which may cause death, but this, of course, is not the reference in this passage. The closest equivalent in some languages is ‘how can death be victorious?’ or ‘death cannot be victorious.’ In some instances it may be necessary to represent the personification as ‘you who cause death,’ and thus this expression in ⟦1 Corinthians 15:55|1 Corinthians 15:55⟧ may be translated as ‘you who cause death will not always be victorious’ or ‘… will not in the end be victorious.’

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Powers
s.d: (an idiom, literally: gates of Hades) death as an impersonal supernatural power
s.c: Some scholars, however, understand πύλαι ᾅδου to mean Satanic powers of evil.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Show Favoritism, Prejudice
s.d: pertaining to not being prejudiced

s.dp: Aspect › Cease, Stop
s.d: pertaining to not ceasing from some continuous activity
s.g: not ceasing; not stopping; unceasingly; continuously

s.dp: Aspect › Cease, Stop
s.d: pertaining to not ceasing from some continuous activity
s.g: not ceasing; not stopping; unceasingly; continuously

s.dp: Violence, Harm, Destroy, Kill › Harm, Wound
s.d: to hurt or to harm, with the implication of doing something which is wrong and undeserved

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Just, Righteous
s.d: to do that which is unjust or unrighteous
s.g: to act unjustly; to do what is wrong

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Treat Badly
s.d: to mistreat by acting unjustly toward someone
s.g: to act unjustly toward; to mistreat
s.c: It is also possible to understand ἀδικέω in ⟦Matthew 20:13|Matthew 20:13⟧ as to act unjustly toward (see LN 88.22).

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Just, Righteous
s.d: (derivative of {L:ἀδικέω<SDBG:ἀδικέω:000001>}[b] ‘to act unjustly,’ {D:88.22}) what is done in an unrighteous or unjust manner

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Just, Righteous
s.d: an activity which is unjust
s.g: unjust deed; unrighteousness; doing what is unjust

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Just, Righteous
s.d: pertaining to not being right or just

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Religious
s.d: a person who is not a member of the Christian community and by implication possibly unjust or not in a right relation with God
s.g: unbeliever; not a follower of Christ

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Just, Righteous
s.d: pertaining to not being right or just

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person in the genealogy of Jesus

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Bad, Evil, Harmful, Damaging
s.d: pertaining to not being in accordance with what is right, appropriate, or fitting
s.g: not fitting; what should not be done; bad

s.dp: Value › Valuable, Lacking in Value
s.d: pertaining to having been proven worthless
s.g: of no value; valueless; worth nothing

s.dp: Features of Objects › Pure, Unadulterated, Undiluted
s.d: pertaining to being pure, with the implication of not being adulterated

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: (derivative of Ἀδραμύττιον ‘Adramyttium,’ not occurring in the NT) pertaining to Adramyttium, a seaport in Mysia

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: body of water between Italy and the Balkan peninsula

s.dp: Sequence
s.d: the first in a series, with implications of significance or importance
s.c: This expression is explained in some manuscripts as ‘the beginning and the end’ and in others as ‘the first and the last’ and in ⟦Revelation 22:13|Revelation 22:13⟧ as both ‘the first and the last’ and ‘the beginning and the end.’ The combination of alpha and omega in secular literature came to designate the entire universe and all kinds of divine and demonic powers, so that in Revelation this title could refer to Christ’s dominion over the universe. In the use of such an expression as ‘the alpha and the omega,’ there is obviously also an important element of status.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Honesty, Sincerity
s.d: the quality of integrity as an expression of moral soundness
